newsitem.title: USA: Fort Worth draws up $178 million bond package.
newsitem.headline: Fort Worth draws up $178 million bond package.

text.p: City officials here drew up a $178 million bond package to finance various capital improvements in the next four years, Assistant City Manager Charles Boswell said on Tuesday.

The city council will begin examining the package this week to identify which of the projects should be included in the bond package, and were asked to approve a proposed Feb 14, 1998, bond vote, Boswell said.
"This would be a four-year program covering 1998 through 2002," he said. "Our projections indicate that we can support up to $120 million without raising the city's tax rate."
The city's property tax rate in the past three years has fallen to $0.95 per $100 valuation from $0.975, but remains one of the highest in Texas.
The city has a AA rating from all three major rating agencies, Boswell said. Neighboring Dallas, with a property tax rate of $0.671 per $100 valuation has a AAA rating.

The bonds would finance street construction, parks, and firefighting, along with three new branch libraries and tourism promotion, including improvements to the city's water garden and zoo and upgrades to the Will Rogers Coliseum and the convention center.

The Will Rogers complex, which hosts popular annual stock show and rodeos, alone could cost up to $20 million if construction of a new arena with facilities for the handicapped is approved. Modernization of the 30-year old convention center could cost more than $40 million.
"I can't predict what the council will decide, but I am assuming that they will want to maintain the tax rate without an increase and so we may have to wait for some of the items," Boswell said.
Voters last approved a $160 million general obligation bond in 1986.

Boswell said the city's total general obligation debt is expected to fall to about $320 million by the end of the fiscal year ending September 30 from more than $340 million at the start of the year. The city has about $16 million left over from previous programs which will be issued next year.
"We will continue to retire more debt than we assume. That is why we believe we can afford this new package without raising the tax rate," he said.
